games.title: Atari Football
games.note: Credited with popularizing the trackball; it was the second highest-earning US arcade game of 1979, after Space Invaders.

games.title: Tehkan World Cup
games.note: A top-down arcade football game played with trackballs.

games.title: MicroProse Soccer
games.note: Sensible Software's first football game, published by MicroProse.

games.title: International Soccer
games.note: A side-on football game sold on cartridge for the Commodore 64.

games.title: FIFA International Soccer
games.note: Led by Bruce McMillan; its isometric view set it apart from top-down rivals. A new FIFA followed every year.

games.title: FIFA: Road to World Cup 98
games.note: Blur's 'Song 2' played over its intro.

games.title: EA Sports FC 24
games.note: The first game after EA's FIFA licence ended; the series carried on under the EA Sports FC name.

games.title: International Superstar Soccer
games.note: The first game in Konami's International Superstar Soccer series.

games.title: Pro Evolution Soccer
games.note: Known as World Soccer Winning Eleven in Japan; the series traces back to 1995's Goal Storm.

games.title: eFootball
games.note: Konami's first football game without the PES name in nearly 20 years, released free-to-play.

games.title: Strat-O-Matic Football
games.note: A dice-and-card football simulation built from real players' statistics.

games.title: John Madden Football
games.note: Took three years to make; John Madden refused to endorse it unless each team had a full 11 players.

games.title: John Madden Football (1990)
games.note: The Mega Drive game that grew into the yearly Madden NFL series.

games.title: Arch Rivals
games.note: Two-on-two arcade basketball where players could punch opponents to steal the ball.

games.title: NBA Jam
games.note: Two-on-two basketball with real NBA players, 'on fire' streaks and impossible dunks.

games.title: NFL Blitz
games.note: Seven-a-side American football with late hits and no penalties.

games.title: NHL Hockey
games.note: Sold in Europe as EA Hockey; the start of EA's yearly NHL series.

games.title: NHL '94
games.note: Still played in fan-run online leagues decades after release.

games.title: Olympic Decathlon
games.note: One of Microsoft's earliest games: the ten decathlon events on early home computers.

games.title: Daley Thompson's Decathlon
games.note: Nicknamed a 'joystick killer' for the frantic waggling its running events demanded.

games.title: California Games
games.note: Swapped Olympic events for half-pipe skateboarding, surfing, BMX, roller skating, footbag and flying disc.

games.title: Wii Fit
games.note: Its Balance Board was inspired by sumo wrestlers, who weigh themselves on two scales at once.

games.title: Ring Fit Adventure
games.note: An exercise game built as an adventure; it has sold over 15 million copies.

games.title: Kinect Sports
games.note: A Kinect launch game: a camera tracked players' whole bodies, with no controller.

games.title: Golf (NES)
games.note: Programmed by Satoru Iwata; a hidden copy was found inside the Nintendo Switch's system software in 2017.

games.title: Everybody's Golf
games.note: Known as Hot Shots Golf in North America; Clap Hanz took over the series from the second game.

games.title: Mario Golf
games.note: Nintendo liked Camelot's prototype so much that it cancelled its own golf game.

games.title: Mario Tennis
games.note: Introduced Waluigi as Wario's doubles partner.

games.title: Leader Board
games.note: A 3D golf game showing each hole from behind the golfer.

games.title: Links: The Challenge of Golf
games.note: Photo-realistic VGA courses, starting with Torrey Pines.

games.title: Windjammers
games.note: A flying-disc duel that found a new competitive scene decades later, including a side tournament at EVO 2018.

games.title: Punch-Out!!
games.note: Used two stacked monitors; Shigeru Miyamoto designed the characters.

games.title: Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!!
games.note: Later reissued as Punch-Out!! with Mr. Dream in place of Tyson.

games.title: Blood Bowl
games.note: A fantasy American football board game with orcs, elves and dice-rolled injuries.

games.title: Missile Command
games.note: When the last city falls, the screen reads 'The End' instead of 'Game Over'.

games.title: Mega-Lo-Mania
games.note: A real-time god game in which rival leaders race up a tech tree from the Stone Age to the nuclear age.

links.took: Atari Football made American football a hit video game, out-earning all but Space Invaders in 1979.
links.added: Full 11-a-side teams, real playbooks and John Madden's endorsement on home computers.

links.took: The trackball, which Atari Football popularized; Dave Theurer programmed its four-player version.
links.added: Theurer's own design: defending cities from falling missiles with a trackball-aimed crosshair.

links.took: Statistics-driven simulation; Trip Hawkins wanted a football game inspired by Strat-O-Matic Football.
links.added: Real-time play on screen with 11 players a side and Madden's playbooks.

links.took: The Madden name, 11-a-side realism and play calling from a playbook.
links.added: Fast console action on the Mega Drive; it became the yearly Madden NFL series.

links.took: Its two-on-two arcade basketball format; Mark Turmell set out to make something similar to Arch Rivals.
links.added: Real NBA stars, digitized graphics, huge dunks and the 'on fire' streak bonus.
links.extra: Turmell: 'My big ideas in NBA Jam were to do the spectacular dunks and two-on-two basketball.'

links.took: Midway's over-the-top arcade sports formula, which it applied to its other sports games.
links.added: Seven-a-side American football with late hits and almost no rules.

links.took: EA's fast arcade-simulation ice hockey on the Mega Drive.
links.added: Both NHL teams and real NHLPA players, the one-timer shot, and arena organ music.
links.extra: NHLPA Hockey '93 came in between; programmer Mark Lesser worked on the one-timer.

links.took: Park Place Productions' Mega Drive sports know-how; its first Genesis game was John Madden Football.
links.added: Fast, physical ice hockey with real NHL teams.

links.took: Its top-down arcade football format, which Chris Yates and Jon Hare adapted.
links.added: Their own additions for home computers, in Sensible Software's first football game.

links.took: Hare and Yates used MicroProse Soccer as the basis for Sensible Soccer.
links.added: Tiny sprites on a zoomed-out pitch for quick passing, and big club and international squads.

links.took: Its tiny sprites: the developers started the game after playing around with Mega-Lo-Mania's sprites.
links.added: A zoomed-out football pitch built for fast passing play.

links.took: Sensible Software's tiny-sprite graphic style from Sensible Soccer.
links.added: Squads of little soldiers sent into battle with a mouse, with dark humour.

links.took: A market leader to beat: EA studied top-down Sensible Soccer and Kick Off, then went another way.
links.added: An isometric view, more realistic players and real national teams.

links.took: Kick Off's fast football, one of the top-down market leaders EA's team studied.
links.added: An isometric camera and a realistic, broadcast-style presentation.

links.took: Fast, fluid football; Wikipedia credits Sensible Soccer with influence on FIFA and Pro Evolution Soccer.
links.added: 3D players, tactical depth and Konami's Master League career mode.

links.took: Konami's ISS football brand, carried by the ISS Pro games that grew into PES.
links.added: Tactical, simulation-style play and the Master League career mode.
links.extra: PES grew from Konami Tokyo's ISS Pro games (1997), which carried the ISS name in Europe.

links.took: Konami's football simulation series.
links.added: A free-to-play model and a new engine, dropping the PES name.

links.took: EA's FIFA series and its licensed national teams.
links.added: Full World Cup qualifying for every FIFA nation, an indoor mode and a licensed song.

links.took: EA's yearly football series, with its clubs, leagues and players.
links.added: A new name after the FIFA licence ended, plus women players in Ultimate Team.
links.extra: Many yearly FIFA games came in between, ending with FIFA 23.

links.took: A decathlon game on home computers, via Starpath's unfinished Sweat! The Decathlon Game.
links.added: Several Olympic sports with an opening ceremony, medals and national flags for up to eight players.
links.extra: Wikipedia says Summer Games came from Sweat!, which Microsoft's Olympic Decathlon had influenced.

links.took: Track & Field popularized multi-event athletics games driven by fast button or joystick action.
links.added: Swimming, diving and gymnastics alongside athletics, for up to eight players at home.

links.took: Its game design and frantic button-mashing running events, per Wikipedia.
links.added: All ten decathlon events, endorsed by Olympic champion Daley Thompson.
links.extra: Wikipedia says the game design was based on Konami's Track & Field.

links.took: Epyx's multi-event 'Games' format with turn-taking for several players.
links.added: Californian sports: half-pipe skateboarding, surfing, BMX, roller skating, footbag and flying disc.

links.took: A place in Miyamoto's original design document for a core group of games including Wii Sports.
links.added: The Balance Board, body measurements and daily exercise routines like yoga.
links.extra: Miyamoto said he and his family had become more health-conscious, tracking their weight.

links.took: Nintendo's exercise-game idea; Wikipedia calls Ring Fit its spiritual successor.
links.added: A Ring-Con and leg strap, and workouts framed as an adventure with battles.

links.took: Wii Sports popularized motion-controlled sports party games for families.
links.added: No controller at all: a camera tracks the player's whole body.

links.took: Nintendo's golf line, which continued in NES Open Tournament Golf before Mario Golf.
links.added: Mario characters with their own shot styles and Camelot's simple swing meter.
links.extra: Mario Golf is the successor to NES Open Tournament Golf (1991), Nintendo's follow-up to Golf.

links.took: Camelot's accessible golf design, first made for Sony as Everybody's Golf.
links.added: Mario characters with distinct power and spin, and four-player Nintendo 64 matches.

links.took: Camelot's approach to Mario sports: simple controls with depth, and characters with distinct types.
links.added: Tennis with charged shots, and the first appearance of Waluigi.

links.took: Access Software's 3D golfer's-eye golf simulation.
links.added: Photo-realistic VGA graphics of real courses, starting with Torrey Pines.

links.took: Pong's two-player volleys: Wikipedia calls its mechanics 'essentially the same as Pong or air hockey'.
links.added: Characters with special throws, wall bounces and goal zones worth different points.

links.took: The fast flying-disc duel and its characters.
links.added: Hand-drawn art, new characters and online play.

links.took: Nintendo's behind-the-boxer view and opponents with patterns to learn.
links.added: A home version starring Little Mac, with a trainer and Mike Tyson as the final bout.

links.took: Games Workshop's board-game rules: turn-based fantasy football decided by dice.
links.added: Online leagues and an optional real-time mode.

links.took: International Soccer popularized football games on home computers.
links.added: A top-down pitch, a ball that runs free of players' feet, and quick passing.
